11.text: Some cases of protest of women against intolerable ill-treatment by the

12.text: fathers-in-law are known to me. For instance, on the Wolverene River I met

13.text: an old man, Omrêlqoˊt by name, who was a rich reindeer-owner. He was

14.text: hospitable even to strangers, but stingy with his own house-mates. Since he

15.text: was quite irascible, this led to quarrels. One summer all the people in the

16.text: neighborhood were short of tobacco, and he alone had a few pounds. He

17.text: distributed the greater part of it among his neighbors, and left almost nothing

18.text: for his own house-mates. Being himself a great smoker, he stopped the supply

19.text: of tobacco of the women of his household. Now, all the people of Arctic

20.text: Siberia would rather go hungry than be without a smoke. “Tobacco is

21.text: shameless,” is a saying of the Russian creoles: “it makes the poorest people

22.text: bold in their demands even upon the chief officer.” Whoever knows the

23.text: abject fear in which Russian creoles hold officers even of inferior rank, will

24.text: appreciate the significance of this saying.

29.text: In dealing with his neighbors, Omrêlqoˊt, to whom I have referred before,

30.text: faithfully followed the general rule which requires, in case of need, that the

31.text: last pipeful be divided or smoked by turns; but the women of his own

32.text: household were not treated so liberally. A quarrel ensued; and one of his

33.text: daughters-in-law, who was also hot-tempered, took up a lance and inflicted on

34.text: the old man three wounds, — one on the shoulder, and two others in the

35.text: back. The old man drew his belt-knife and seriously wounded his assailant.

36.text: The end of the quarrel was, that the woman left the camp of her husband

37.text: and father-in-law, and went back to her own people. But Omrêlqoˊt was

38.text: called ever after, to his great ire and horror, “that one pricked by a woman.”
